title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyl compounds
keyIdea: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar: the carbon is δ+ and the oxygen δ−. A nucleophile (CN⁻ from KCN, or H⁻ from NaBH₄) uses its lone pair to attack the δ+ carbon; at the same time the π electrons of C=O move onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide intermediate with O⁻. The O⁻ then takes H⁺ (from dilute acid or water) to form an OH group. CN⁻ gives a hydroxynitrile with one more carbon; H⁻ reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. The C=O group is planar, so attack from either face is equally likely: aldehydes and unsymmetrical ketones give a racemic mixture of enantiomers.

kid: In C=O, oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself. So the carbon is a bit positive, δ+. The oxygen is a bit negative, δ−. A nucleophile has a lone pair it can give. It goes for the δ+ carbon.

Step one has two curly arrows. The lone pair on the carbon of CN⁻ moves to the δ+ carbon. That makes a new C–C bond. At the same time, the π pair of C=O moves onto the oxygen. Now we have an alkoxide ion, with O⁻. Step two: a lone pair on O⁻ grabs H⁺. The O⁻ becomes OH.

KCN, then dilute acid, makes a hydroxynitrile. The chain gains one carbon. Propanal has 3 carbons, so it gives 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, with 4. NaBH₄ gives the hydride ion, H⁻, as the nucleophile. An aldehyde turns into a primary alcohol. A ketone turns into a secondary alcohol.

The C=O carbon is flat. So the nucleophile can hit from above or below, with equal odds. Say the new carbon has four different groups. Then each side gives a different enantiomer. They form 50:50. That is a racemic mixture, and it does not rotate polarised light.
adult: This is AQA A-level Chemistry 3.3.8, aldehydes and ketones. OCR A 6.1.2 and Edexcel Topic 17 match it. Students outline the mechanism for reduction by NaBH₄, with the nucleophile shown as H⁻. They outline the mechanism with KCN, then dilute acid. They explain why it can give a mixture of enantiomers. KCN is very toxic, and acid releases HCN gas. So the hazard and the fume cupboard are part of the content too.

Terms to use: carbonyl, polar bond, δ+ and δ−, nucleophile, lone pair and curly arrow. Add π bond, alkoxide intermediate, protonation and hydroxynitrile. In names, the nitrile carbon counts as C1. Then reduction, primary and secondary alcohol, and trigonal planar. Last come chiral centre, enantiomer and racemic mixture.

Common mistakes: sending the nucleophile to the δ− oxygen. Starting an arrow on an atom, not on a lone pair or bond. Drawing the cyanide attack from nitrogen. Moving the π pair onto carbon. Forgetting the protonation step. Naming the product with the old chain length. And saying a racemic product has no chiral centre. In fact both enantiomers form, in equal amounts, so their effects on light cancel.

Contrast this with electrophilic addition to C=C. That bond is non-polar and rich in electrons. So it draws electrophiles such as Br₂, HBr and H₂SO₄. The C=O carbon is poor in electrons, so it draws nucleophiles. In the lab, students attack three carbonyls and draw both arrows. They protonate and name three products. They run attacks on each face and sort attackers by target bond.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to draw the mechanism for propanal with KCN then dilute acid from memory, and to explain why the product does not rotate polarised light even though it has a chiral centre.

visual.caption: Which product forms? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: aim CN⁻ and H⁻ at the δ+ carbon, draw the curly arrows, protonate and name the product, attack the flat C=O from both faces.

practice.prompt: Which atom does the cyanide ion attack in propanal?
choices: The hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon
practice.hint: Oxygen is more electronegative. Which atom is left electron-poor?
practice.explain: Oxygen pulls the C=O electrons, so the carbonyl carbon is δ+. The nucleophile's lone pair is attracted to it.

practice.prompt: An aldehyde with {n} carbon atoms reacts with KCN, then dilute acid. How many carbon atoms are in the hydroxynitrile?
practice.hint: The cyanide ion brings its own carbon, and a new C–C bond forms.
practice.explain: CN⁻ adds one carbon, so {n} carbons become {=n+1}. The nitrile carbon is counted in the name.

practice.prompt: In the first step, where does the curly arrow from the C=O π bond point?
practice.hint: Which atom can best hold a negative charge?
practice.explain: The π pair moves onto the more electronegative oxygen, giving the alkoxide O⁻.

practice.prompt: A ketone with {n} carbon atoms is reduced with NaBH₄. How many carbon atoms are in the alcohol formed?
practice.explain: H⁻ adds only hydrogen, so the secondary alcohol still has {n} carbons.

pool.prompt: What is the intermediate in nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl?
pool.hint: Where do the π electrons end up after the first step?
pool.explain: The π pair moves onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide ion. A carbocation belongs to electrophilic addition to C=C.

pool.prompt: What forms when butanone is reduced with NaBH₄?
pool.hint: Butanone is a ketone. Where is its C=O?
pool.explain: Ketones reduce to secondary alcohols; the OH stays on carbon 2, giving butan-2-ol.

pool.prompt: Why does ethanal with KCN then dilute acid give a racemic mixture?
choices: The planar C=O is attacked equally from both faces
The product has no chiral centre
Cyanide only attacks from one side
pool.hint: Think about the shape around the carbonyl carbon.
pool.explain: The carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar, so attack from each face is equally likely, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers.

pool.prompt: Which product of KCN, then dilute acid, is NOT chiral?
pool.hint: Look for a carbon with four different groups.
pool.explain: Propanone gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile: the carbon has two CH₃ groups, so it is not a chiral centre.

pool.prompt: Why does Br₂ add to ethene but not to the C=O of propanone?
choices: C=C is electron-rich and attracts electrophiles; the C=O carbon is δ+
pool.hint: Is Br₂ looking for electrons or giving them?
pool.explain: Br₂ acts as an electrophile, attracted to the electron-rich C=C. The δ+ carbonyl carbon attracts nucleophiles instead.

pool.prompt: {n} molecules of propanal are each attacked once by CN⁻ from a random face. About how many give each enantiomer?
pool.explain: Equal chance for each face means about {=n/2} of each enantiomer: a racemic mixture.

pool.prompt: A hydroxynitrile with {n} carbon atoms was made from an aldehyde with KCN, then dilute acid. How many carbon atoms did the aldehyde have?
pool.explain: Take away the nitrile carbon: the aldehyde had {=n-1} carbons.

pool.prompt: In the protonation step, where does the curly arrow start?
choices: On a lone pair of the O⁻
pool.hint: Arrows start on electrons. Which species has a spare pair?
pool.explain: The O⁻ lone pair forms the new O–H bond, so the arrow runs from that lone pair to H⁺.
